mem.t: I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.

lessons.title: A Book of Joy Written in Prison
lessons.theme: In chains, Paul wrote a letter brimming with joy

v: I thank my God whenever I remember you,
always in every request of mine on behalf of you all, making my requests with joy,
for your partnership in furtherance of the Good News from the first day until now;
being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.
For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.

lessons.still: Imagine yourself sitting beside Paul — a bare prison cell, yet filled with thanksgiving. Be still for a moment, and bring before the Lord whatever situation makes you feel “trapped” right now. Say, “Lord, you are here, so I can rejoice.”
teach: Some flowers bloom only at night; the darkness actually brings out their fragrance. Philippians is that kind of letter. Paul wrote it in chains, his future uncertain, yet “joy” appears again and again. This week we will work slowly through the book using the four Bible-reading steps we learned in the first stage: Read, Reflect, Pray, Do.

The church at Philippi was the first church Paul planted in Europe (Acts 16). Its first members included Lydia, the seller of purple cloth; a slave girl set free from a spirit; and the jailer who came to faith after hearing Paul and Silas singing hymns at midnight. Whenever Paul remembered them he gave thanks, because of their “partnership in furtherance of the Good News,” and he was confident God “will complete it.” The key sentence of the whole book is: “For to me to live is Christ.”

Paul's joy did not depend on his circumstances but on a single focus: Christ. In chapter 1 he says his chains have actually advanced the gospel (1:12), and even when some preach Christ out of envy, he rejoices (1:18). Those focused on themselves feel wronged at every turn; those focused on Christ see God at work at every turn. This week, let us ask the Lord to bring our focus back into line as well.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Focus on Jesus — not on yourself, not on others, not on your circumstances. Paul lived this out in prison. “To live is Christ” is the self-emptied life itself: it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. The self-emptied life is not loss; it is entry into the limitless.
q: Who is God? — The God who “will complete it” — what unfinished work is he doing in you right now?
Who am I? — Right now, is the focus of your life Christ, yourself, other people, or your circumstances?
How shall I respond? — Like Paul, how can you find reasons for thanksgiving in today's “chains”?
lessons.jesus: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus told his disciples he wanted his joy to remain in them (John 15:11). The cross was right before him, yet his joy was not taken away, because his focus was on the Father's will. Paul's joy came from this very Lord.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that he who began a good work in me will complete it. Turn my focus away from my circumstances and away from myself, back to you. May I too be able to say, “For to me to live is Christ,” and give thanks for your work even in hard places. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: This week, read through the four chapters of Philippians over four days, using Read, Reflect, Pray, Do
Write down something that makes you feel trapped, and next to it write one thing you are thankful for
Thank God for a partner who shares with you in furthering the gospel — and tell them
lessons.noon: “For to me to live is Christ.” — Lord, right now I turn my focus back to you.

lessons.title: Having the Mind of Christ
lessons.theme: The secret of unity is counting others better than yourself

v: doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.
Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name,
that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth,
and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

lessons.still: Quietly bring to mind someone who has recently made you uncomfortable. Don't rush to sort out who was right; simply place them before the Lord and say, “Lord, put your mind in me, so that I count them better than myself.”
teach: Two goats meet on a narrow log bridge. If both insist on crossing first, they both fall into the river; if one lies down and lets the other step over, both reach the far bank safely. Pride stirs up pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win. The church at Philippi had its quarrels too (4:2), and Paul's remedy was the mind of Christ.

In the first week we read 2:5–8 and saw Christ emptying himself. Today we look at what comes before and after. Before it are commands: no rivalry, no conceit, “each counting others better than himself.” After it comes the outcome: God “highly exalted him,” and every knee will bow to him. Christ's descent was not defeat but the road to glory — and that road is our road too.

“Counting others better than himself” does not mean pretending to think little of yourself; it means choosing to put others' needs first, looking “also to the things of others.” The self-ruled heart asks, “What do I get?” The mind of Christ asks, “What can I give?” Here is the change of mindset: unity does not depend on everyone agreeing, but on each person being willing to bow low first.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is laying down power and returning to our place. Christ emptied himself, and God highly exalted him; when we let Jesus reign, we no longer need to grab for empty glory. This passage ends “to the glory of God the Father” — letting Jesus receive all the glory is our end point too.
q: Who is God? — God exalted the Christ who humbled himself. What does that show you about God?
Who am I? — In which relationship are you competing for “conceit,” for empty glory?
How shall I respond? — How can you concretely look “to the things of others” today?
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper the disciples were still arguing over who was greatest, yet Jesus said, “I am in the middle of you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27). He did not crush their pride with authority; he healed it with his own humility.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet you willingly humbled yourself. Put your mind in me, so that I stop chasing empty glory and gladly count others better than myself. Wherever I am contending with others, teach me to bow low first, so that God the Father is glorified. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: In a discussion, ask for the other person's view before giving your own
Bless, in a concrete way, someone you have been quietly comparing yourself with
Do one thing that looks “to the things of others,” expecting nothing in return
lessons.noon: “But in humility, each counting others better than himself” — Lord, right now let me bow low first.

lessons.title: Forgetting What Is Behind, Straining Toward What Is Ahead
lessons.theme: Treasuring the knowledge of Christ above all, and pressing on toward the goal

v: However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ.

Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ
Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before,
I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Open your hands and imagine them holding your past achievements and your past hurts. Lay them down one by one, telling the Lord, “I give all of these to you.” Then, with empty hands, lift your head and look ahead to the Lord.
teach: A runner who keeps looking back will either stumble or fall behind; a runner clutching a trophy can't run fast. In chapter 3 Paul lists the credentials he once took pride in — his pedigree, his righteousness under the law, his religious zeal — and then says he considers all of it “a loss.”

Paul uses a merchant's bookkeeping language: “gain” and “loss.” The credentials once listed in the income column are all moved to the loss column, even counted as “refuse,” because he has found the supreme treasure: the knowledge of Christ Jesus his Lord. “Forgetting the things which are behind” is not amnesia; it means no longer letting past successes or failures define us. “Stretching forward” means running hard toward God's upward call.

The self-ruled life often lives in the past. Living in past glory, we grow proud; living in past hurts, we grow bitter; living in past failures, we sink into self-pity. All three are focused on self. Here is the change of mindset: my worth is not in my past but in Christ; my direction is not behind me but in God's upward call.
lessons.light: 321 Light: This is a change of perspective — from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal. Paul exchanged “a righteousness of my own” for the righteousness that comes through faith in Christ (3:9). This is the self-emptied life: laying down our own capital and gaining the riches of Christ. The self-emptied life is not having nothing; it is treasuring Christ above all.
q: Who is God? — Knowing Christ was worth so much that Paul counted everything else as loss. Have you experienced how precious he is?
Who am I? — What do you most often look back on — past glory, past hurts, or past failures?
How shall I respond? — What one thing “behind” will you lay down today so you can run forward?
lessons.jesus: Jesus, “for the joy that was set before him, endured the cross, despising its shame” (Hebrews 12:2). His eyes were fixed on the Father's will and the glory to come. As we run our race, we too look to Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are my greatest treasure. I give you my past achievements, and I give you my past hurts and failures too. Free me from being bound by what lies behind, and help me run single-mindedly toward your call. Knowing you is my supreme treasure. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Draw a line: on the left write “counted as loss,” on the right write “supreme treasure”
Today, when an old wound comes to mind, turn your thoughts and say, “I am running forward.”
Write down one direction in which God is calling you upward this year
lessons.noon: “Forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before” — Lord, right now I run toward you.

lessons.title: Rejoice in the Lord Always
lessons.theme: Joy is not a mood but a choice we make in the Lord

v: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”
Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand.
In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Name the worries in your heart one by one, and after each one add, “Thank you, Lord.” When you have finished, be still for a minute, and let the peace of God that surpasses all understanding stand like a guard at the door of your heart.
teach: A thermometer only reflects the temperature around it; a thermostat changes the temperature of the room. Many people's joy is like a thermometer — up when things are good, down when things are bad. Paul wants us to be thermostats: “Rejoice in the Lord always.” Notice: “in the Lord” — not in our circumstances, and not in ourselves.

This passage has a clear order: joy (toward God) → gentleness (toward others) → not being anxious (toward ourselves) → prayer, petition and thanksgiving (entrusting) → peace (God's response). “Guard” is originally a military word for a garrison holding a city. When we hand over our worries, God's peace stands guard over our hearts and thoughts in Christ Jesus.

“In nothing be anxious” does not tell us to be irresponsible; it tells us not to let worry sit in the master's seat. Worry is actually a hidden form of the self-ruled life: I want to control the outcome myself. Thanksgiving, by contrast, acknowledges that God is in charge. Live from the heart by the Spirit and you have peace; live from the head by yourself and worry grows.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Live from the heart and you find joy; live from the head and you find worry. Turning worry into prayer is laying down power and letting God be God; adding thanksgiving lets Jesus receive the glory. Those who give thanks in everything find that their joy no longer rises and falls with their circumstances.
q: Who is God? — “The Lord is at hand.” How does this change the way you see your difficulties?
Who am I? — Is your joy more like a thermometer or a thermostat?
How shall I respond? — Which worry will you hand to God today with “prayer + thanksgiving”?
lessons.jesus: As the storm raged and the disciples panicked, Jesus was asleep in the stern on a cushion (Mark 4:38). His peace did not come from the absence of storms but from complete trust in the Father. This Lord lives in us, and his peace becomes the guard at the door of our hearts.
lessons.pray: Lord, I hand you the worries in my heart one by one. Thank you that you are in control of everything and that you are near. Guard my heart and my thoughts with your peace that surpasses all understanding, so that today I rejoice in you always and treat others with gentleness. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Turn one worry into a written prayer, and add a line of thanks
Today, whenever a complaint is about to come out, first say, “Thank you, Lord”
With a gentle heart, let someone else go first in some small matter
lessons.noon: “Rejoice in the Lord always!” — Lord, right now I choose to rejoice in you.

lessons.title: The Secret of Doing All Things
lessons.theme: The secret of contentment lies not in our circumstances but in the Lord who strengthens us

v: Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it.
I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In any and all circumstances I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need.
I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.
My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Quietly count what you have right now, and also admit what you lack. Place both in the Lord's hands and say, “Lord, plenty and want are both in your hands; leaning on you is enough for me.”
teach: Philippians 4:13 is often printed on sports jerseys, as if it meant, “If I just have enough faith, I'll win the game.” But read the context and you find that the “all things” Paul means are being humbled and abounding, being hungry and being filled. This is not a slogan for success; it is the secret of contentment.

Paul says contentment is something he has “learned”; it did not come naturally. The word “secret” originally referred to being initiated into a mystery. Between plenty and hunger he learned that strength lies not in circumstances but in “him who strengthens me.” Verse 19 says God will supply “according to his riches in glory” — not according to our desires, but according to his riches and his good purpose.

The self-ruled life measures God by circumstances: in good times, God is good; in hard times, God is absent. Those living the self-emptied life lean on the Lord in every situation — not proud in plenty, not complaining in want. This week in Philippians we have seen that joy, humility, pressing on and contentment all flow from “to live is Christ.” Next week we will learn confession and forgiveness through prayer, so that this life can put down even deeper roots.
lessons.light: 321 Light: “Through Christ” is the centre of the whole verse — not “I can,” but “through him.” The self-ruled life says, “I can”; the self-emptied life says, “The Lord can, and through him I can.” This is the self-emptied life overcoming the self-ruled life. The glory goes not to a capable me but to the Lord who gives strength.
q: Who is God? — How has the God who supplies according to his riches in glory provided for you in a time of need?
Who am I? — In which situation — plenty or want — do you find it hardest to be content?
How shall I respond? — In what matter today will you say, “Through the Lord, I can”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20), yet he never lacked the Father's presence. He said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34). His contentment flowed from his relationship with the Father.
lessons.pray: Lord who gives me strength, I confess that on my own I can do nothing. Thank you for being with me in plenty and in want. Teach me the secret of contentment — not proud in plenty, not complaining in want — leaning on you in everything and giving the glory to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down one thanksgiving from a time of plenty and one from a time of want
Share with a spiritual companion the verse from Philippians that touched you most this week
lessons.noon: “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.” — Lord, right now I lean on you.
